newsitem.title: PERU: Peru frees 28 people unjustly jailed for terrorism.
newsitem.headline: Peru frees 28 people unjustly jailed for terrorism.

text.p: The Peruvian government released on Friday 28 more innocent prisoners among the estimated hundreds jailed unjustly during the state's ongoing war against communist guerrillas.
"We believe we are going some way to making amends for the judicial mistakes committed in condemning innocent people," said Justice Minister Carlos Hermoza Moya.
A decree, published in the government daily El Peruano and signed by President Alberto Fujimori, granted "pardons to various people condemned for crimes of terrorism or betrayal of the fatherland."

It followed Tuesday's release of three journalists, who were the first to benefit from recommendations of a new government-appointed commission charged with examining the cases for pardons among more than 3,000 people in jail on terrorism charges.

The government, which has since 1995 released nearly 250 innocent prisoners wrongly accused of terrorism, admits that up to 400 more could still be unfairly behind bars. Human rights groups, however, say the number could be as high as 1,000.

At the Chorrillos women's prison in Lima, where six of the 28 were freed, there were emotional scenes as those inmates due to be released joined hands and sang together in a final act of solidarity before walking to freedom.
"I am going to pray for the people who freed me," muttered 60-year-old Liduvina Caqui, a Quechuan-speaking indigenous woman sentenced to 15 years' in 1992.

Another woman, Santosa Lopez Flores, 40, released after three years' in the Chorillos penitentiary, hugged her daughter as she told how she was tortured by police to sign the confession that formed the basis of her conviction.
Friday's decree said the latest releases were based on "the reasonable presumption that (the prisoners) had no type of link with terrorist elements, activities or organisations."

Peruvian ombudsman Jorge Santistevan y de Noriega, one of three members of the commission recommending pardons, promised the body would work "24 hours a day, weekends, all the time" to ensure "the freedom deserved by those people ... who received such drastic sentences on such flimsy evidence."
He called for a relaxation of anti-terrorism legislation and an end to the functions of "faceless" courts responsible for most of the wrong convictions.
Conflicts sparked by the Maoist Shining Path rebels and the smaller Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) have cost 30,000 lives and $25 billion in infrastructure damage since 1980.

Although greatly weakened since the 1992 capture of its leader Abimael Guzman, Shining Path has icreasingly flexed its muscles this year with a series of car-bombs, assassinations and clashes with security forces.
